Mr. Speaker,
I have reliable information that a large number of workmen are stranded at The Pas and are in a serious condition. speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend I
may say that arrangements are now being made to secure the personnel of the working force for the construction work at Churchill during the coming season. About 80 per cent of the men who were there last year have expressed their willingness to go back, and they will be given the preference. At the present time a representative of the department is in western Canada endeavouring to secure the balance of the men, and in the course of a few days he will be at The Pas. Unfortunately, it appears that a large number of men went to The Pas in the expectation that they might find employment in the north country.
I may add for the information of the house that in the near future the Canadian National Railways will be resuming the work they have to do on the line to Fort Churchill and several hundred men will be required for that work. As to what else can be done in that matter, I am at the moment not able to say.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, May 14, consideration of the motion of Hon. Charles A. Dunning that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, the amendment thereto of Mr. Bennett, and -the amendment to the amendment thereto of Mr. Fansher (Last Mountain).

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is nothing in parliamentary life which can transcend the importance of the budget, and there is nothing which better reveals in a temporary fashion the mentality of hon. members in the house than the budget debate. There is nothing in our deliberations which has such great effect upon the life of the country as the budget, and the one presented this year is certainly no exception to the rule. It has been introduced by a new Minister of Finance, young in years but who has had a varied and wide experience, and I think it is not an exaggeration to say that the country waited with intense curiosity to learn
21 IS
The Budget-Mr. Glen

the proposals which would be contained in his first budget. He most certainly has provoked thought and discussion. He has not pleased all his friends; on the contrary he has unleashed the political enmity of all his Tory friends. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has run true to form in that he has at least supplied the storm centre of political controversy and I am sure his position is not an unhappy one.
There are two ways, among others, in which the budget can be discussed and appraised. The first is the proposals as contained in the budget itself, and the second is the attitude of the opposition towards those proposals as revealed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). I propose for a few moments to discuss the latter aspect of the situation. At the outset I must say that I cannot reconcile the words of the leader of the opposition when he spoke at the close of the address by the Minister of Finance. I take the view, and I think the country will do likewise, that in the exasperation of the moment he revealed his true deep-seated antagonism to the proposals contained in the budget, and he could only resort to denunciation of anything contained therein. In one breath he deplored the fact that the Minister of Finance had not realized that the word " countervailing " was just a poor substitute for the word "retaliation." In the next sentence he stated that the finance minister had enunciated a tariff policy made in Washington for operation in Canada, and asked whether the Minister of Finance realized that this was nothing more than a retaliatory policy. It is beyond belief that a tariff policy could be framed in Washington as a retaliatory policy for Canada against the United States. Surely the United States are not so blind to their own interests that they will deliberately evolve a tariff against us for the purpose of providing us with a retaliatory weapon. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition omitted to state that we have a section in our customs tariff at the present time which provides for countervailing duties. I shall take the liberty of reading it:
If the president of the United States under authority of the United States Tariff Act of 1922 determines to reduce the duties imposed by such act on the following articles, that is to say, cattle, wheat, wheat flour, oats, barley, potatoes, onions, turnips, hay, fish as enumerated in paragraphs 717, 718, 719 and 720 of the Tariff Act of 1892.
The governor in council may by order in council make such reductions of duties on such articles imported into Canada from the United States as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for such reductions on Canadian products imported into the United States.
[Mr. Glea.1
I think the leader of the opposition must have omitted that from his address. If I have correctly interpreted the address given by that hon. gentleman and the address delivered by his red-blooded colleague the member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), I think I am justified in having assumed that the Tory party are wedded and entirely committed to a policy of reprisals against the United States. Their aim and purpose, as they have declared, is not to turn the other cheek to the United States.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend. The hon. gentleman will recall that last year I distinctly said just the opposite. I said that I was not concerned with legislation against anyone but that I proposed legislation for Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend may turn
as he will. He is in favour of tariffs for Canada against whom? There was only one country with which we were dealing in the discussion which took place last year and that country was the United States. The only reprisals which could have been made against a country at that time would have been against the United States. As a matter of fact hon. members will remember that the leader of the opposition asked that this house should sit until the United States framed their tariff in order that we would be in a position to meet it. If that be so, then on their own submission, these countervailing duties being retaliatory, are exactly what they desired should be done and for that reason would not be framed in Washington. It was rather striking to find-and I give this statement of fact to the house, leaving hon. members to draw their own conclusions-that on the 2nd day of May, the day after the budget was introduced, there was a discussion in the House of Representatives on the proposed duties on certain kinds of timber, lumber and shingles which were restored to the free List. In the course of the debate Representative Crisp is reported on page 8501 of the Congressional Record as follows:
I called attention yesterday to the protests being made by the foreign nations, and in the press to-day you will read where the government of Canada in its budget yesterday raised its tariff rates and raised them to be retaliatory equal to the rates in the present bill, with the statement that if this goes into effect they will be raised to be on a parity with this law.
Canada is our best customer. One of the things we do get from Canada is lumber, and when you stop buying anything from Canada, you are going to lose one of your best customers. You can not blame them for the action they have taken, because that is human nature. Under their budget they are to give preferential tariff nates to other nations that give them pre-

The Budget-Mr. Glen
ferential rates. Consequently commerce will go from those other nations to Canada, and America will lose one of her very best customers.
Gentlemen, you are carrying the tariff to a fanatical state. You have got to think. Are we now having great Republican prosperity? If you would listen to the members of this house talk about the unemployment in their districts you would not think we had much of the boasted Republican prosperity in this country.
Gentlemen, I fear this: If you stop all foreign markets for your surplus goods, whether agricultural or manufactured goods, you are going to have more men out of employment in this country, because the factories are going to shut down.
It is somewhat noteworthy to find such sentiments expressed in that house and I think I have heard like expressions in this house. I cannot and I will not say that a tariff war is in the best interests of Canada. Last year I spoke during the budget debate and I deplored the fact that a tariff war could exist between this country and any other country. To my mind a tariff war is equally as ofen-sive as an armed crusade. Armaments can be curtailed but I think it is more difficult under our system of government to curtail the activities of vested interests, as they are called, in a tariff economic war. People are so ready to believe that when you take away from someone something which he already has you take away a vested interest and therefore it is much more difficult to discontinue a tariff war. I was very much impressed by one fact in connection with the United States tariff. There was a memorial presented by a thousand economists of the highest standing in the United States, protesting against the recently proposed tariff increases. This memorial points out especially that tariffs have not helped agriculture. On May 12 last an Associated Press despatch from Geneva states that the British Labour government is ready for further negotiations looking to a tariff truce. Thirty states which met under the auspices of the League of Nations were unable to agree to a tariff truce, but they adopted a convention under which in principle they recognized the interdependence of their own tariff policies and those of other countries, and undertook to consider the interests of other countries before introducing tariff increases, "except in cases where the urgent and vital interests of national economy render this impossible."
I believe that the next great international question will be the reduction of tariffs, and the question of disarmament necessarily must be linked up with the question of tariff reduction. Both questions concern wars which vitally affect civilization and the burden of which ultimately must fall upon the shoulders
of the people. For that reason I would view with alarm the suggestion that at the next Imperial conference this country should be represented by a protectionist party. They would go to that conference with preconceived notions with regard to tariffs which I profoundly believe are inimical and harmful to the best interests of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask whether that same principle should not apply on this continent as well, instead of building a tariff wall between Canada and the United States?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have already explained that I am entirely in agreement with that view, and I deplore any tariff wall between Canada and any other country. The leader of the opposition dealt at length with the British preference. He had unlimited time at his disposal, but since my time is rather limited I must deal with this question more generally than I should have liked.
Would it be an exaggeration to say that the leader of the opposition is opposed to the British preference, or would it be more delicate to say that he views it with disfavour? His party always has assumed the ultra-British attitude, which being translated into action finds his party, because of party policy only, opposed to the British preference. It is difficult to conceive the Conservative party adopting any other attitude. Their whole policy is protection, and surely it cannot be gainsaid that any measure of free trade with Great Britain or any other country is the absolute negation of their tariff policy as we know it to-day.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is your policy?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will come to my policy
presently. Despite the lip loyalty frequently expressed by the Conservative party they dare any other parties to seek approval of the British preference. I have no doubt the leader of the opposition realizes that our intangible bonds of love and affection with the mother country can be expressed in the more tangible bonds of trade and commerce, and we can make it clear through the British preference that we mean to cement those bonds. Personally I must approve of the provisions of the budget which are expected to result in greater trade with Great Britain. There are absurdities in the present tariff which the Minister of Finance proposes to adjust, and I think it somewhat unfair of opposition speakers to criticize the deletion of some of these items from the customs schedule.
The Budget-Mr. Glen

The budget speech of the Minister of Finance is not only a challenge to other countries; certainly it is a challenge to Great Britain as well. Here we have probably the most far-reaching proposal for reciprocal trade between Canada and the British Isles that ever has been made. Canada now offers to free trade Great Britain a large measure of fre* trade proposals. It is eminently fitting that this offer should come from the present administration, and I make that statement sincerely. We are perhaps too near the events of the last four years to estimate correctly the tremendous and far-reaching consequences of the change in our relationship with the rest of the empire, but I am confident that the present administration, and particularly the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice, will be remembered in the future history of Canada as the proponents and supporters of the new era of empire relationship which was inaugurated at the Imperial conference of 1926, with the consent and the concurrence of the whole British Empire, among whose delegates were the most distinguished statesmen of Great Britain. Now, just before another Imperial conference, Canada has flung out its challenge to Great Britain and the empire to consolidate that forward step by doing away with many of the obstacles in the way of empire trade and commerce. I do think that the present Prime Minister and Minister of Justice are the proper persons to represent Canada at that conference and to complete the work which they began.
In conjunction with this it is a happy augury that the Hudson Bay railway is so near completion and that very soon we will be able to use that route in marketing our grain and other products. In this connection I might add that the people of the west will indignantly resent any efforts which may be made to hinder the full development of the facilities of that railway. For forty years they have been fighting to obtain it and, having obtained it, they hope now that the dice will not be loaded against the Hudson Bay railway as was the case in the past. They look for the full development of the facilities of that route, with the fullest cooperation of government and railway officials.
If these and the other subjects to which I have referred were all that the budget contained I would be in a happy state of mind;
I would cheerfully acquiesce in and support the general principles contained in the budget.
I realize, however, in common with nearly 
every other member who has spoken in this debate, that the tremendous number of changes in the tariff dealing with the iron and steel schedules, among others, must be explained in committee. It is not possible for one who is not an expert, with life long experience, to understand the ramifications of this involved industry. In committee we will have an opportunity to discuss these changes more intelligently, and all that can be done in the meantime is to discuss the general principle. I have received calculations showing the number of items in which the consumers are concerned which are affected by this budget. The figure is very large, and I certainly hope it can be proved. If the Minister of Finance can demonstrate to the house that the figures are even approximately correct it will go far to substantiate his arguments contained in the budget speech.
There are two items, however, which I must discuss as fully as time will permit; I refer to the items dealing with butter and fruits and vegetables, with which I might join the item of eggs. I know my hon. friend the leader of the opposition will be waiting with some interest to learn just what I have to say on this particular subject, in view of my position in the past. I will not keep him long in suspense; I will tell him that my conceptions of what I believe to be sound economic principles are absolutely unchanged, but I am sorry to say that a number of hon. gentlemen-and I hope a small number-have seen fit to change their opinions in this regard. When the Australian treaty, with its extension to New Zealand, was discussed in this house recently I was frankly amazed at the trend of opinion expressed by hon. members. Having that in mind, I was not so greatly surprised on my visit home during the Easter recess to learn that this opinion was shared in part by some of the farmers of the west.
I find it necessary to express my views in this regard; I would be remiss in my duty and false to myself if I did not do so.
I believe that the duty which has been placed on Australian and New Zealand butter represents a shortsighted policy, as far as the interests of western Canada are concerned. If the trade returns from 1923 to l929 are any criterion, not only do those who favour this duty deprive themselves of the right to protest against tariff" duties affecting other industries, but there will be no corresponding benefit to the producers of butter. speechtext:
Are the prices quoted by the
hon. member based on the price of cream as obtaining in Toronto, or upon the price of butter itself?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They are based upon the average monthly Toronto price of No. 1 cream, given in cents per pound for butter fat.
When the time comes that we are exporting butter, then it will be true that the export
market price will become the domestic market price. The point is that you will not make cream shippers richer by shutting out imports, because just so long as our exports of dairy products exceed our imports then the price received by producers for cream or anything else will depend upon the prices ruling on the markets of the world. It is natural for a producer to accept the statements made to him by interested parties and to believe that were it not for the importation of certain quantities of butter he would receive a better price for his commodity. In this particular instance, I think that belief is answered, and I do not believe the producer will derive a cent of benefit.
For many years there has been a persistent agitation waged by the fruit and vegetable growers. They, like the producers of butter, thought that a little protection would benefit their industry, and so far they have been successful. Now, in return, that policy has had an effect more far-reaching than they ever dreamed and with consequences so hazardous that they begin now to tremble. As I have said before, you must be prepared for strange sequels once you begin to wallow in the protectionist trough. One often hears the statement made that the imposition of a tariff does not increase the price to the consumer. In this present instance we have an illuminating and striking example of the actions of those who seek and invoke tariff protection. It has been reported that the fruit jobbers have increased the price of oranges by ten cents per dozen. An outcry was raised immediately, yet the plain truth is that oranges are not included in the budget proposal: they are in the same position as they were prior to its introduction. I have been informed that there is a scarcity of oranges, but I wish the consumer in western Canada could be convinced of that. Does western Canada realize what will ensue if they begin to flirt with tariff protection? I believe that the effect of the tariff on fruits and vegetables undoubtedly will qualify and reconsolidate low tariff opinion in the west.
The Conservatives cannot complain; it is their doctrine. If they were in power they would unhesitatingly increase the tariffs in every direction. So far as we in the west are concerned, we hope that the lesson derived from this temporary tariff expedient will demonstrate the folly of the principle of protection. So far as I am concerned personally, I must oppose the principle involved in these items. I cannot ask for protection on butter in one breath, and in the next seek free trade in fruits and vegetables. The policy
The Budget-Mr. Glen

hitherto obtaining in the west is the only policy suitable to that section of the country- instead of an increasing there shall be a lessening of the burden of the farmers. The grain situation has impaired the revenues of the government, a deficiency in purchasing power has been caused by extraordinary world conditions, and instead of burdening the farmers, relief should be offered to them if they are to live and prosper, and that prosperity cannot be achieved by protection.
This budget contains a variety of items so complex in their character, so diversified in their application that it is impossible to say yea or nay to the budget as a whole. I can support many of the items, but there are others of which I cannot foretell the effect. I doubt if there is a single hon. member in this house who can truthfully say that he knows what will be the effect of all these items. He cannot know that until they have been thoroughly explained. I venture to say that no budget at any time, and certainly not this one, could be answered by yea or nay, and yet we are faced with that necessity. The thought has been expressed in this house many times that there is a better way of dealing with this matter, to have all the items discussed and then a vote taken. In that way we could give a yea or nay, but at the present time all that we know is that we are faced with a proposition which is bound to have far-reaching effects upon the economic life of this country, and in particular upon the economic life of western Canada. I would hate to turn down anything which might be of benefit, but I am faced with the necessity of making a decision on certain principles, the effect of which we do not know. The budget should be put before the house in such a way as to permit intelligent discussion.
I am not satisfied with all the provisions of the budget, but I am convinced that there are many things in it which will be of incaleu-able benefit to the country. What does that reservation mean? It means that I must support the budget.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not think the Conservatives have any reason to complain because they have stated they must have an opportunity of discussing all the items comprised in the budget. I have not heard any members on the Conservative benches state that they understood all the budget and that they could say yea or nay. I know from information gleaned in the lobbies, many members on the Tory side are just as concerned about the budget proposals as any member on this side. I know many members of the Tory party who, if they had an opportunity, and if they consulted their own interests, would vote against their party, but like the rest of us they have to wait until the house goes into committee to ascertain just exactly what the proposals mean. For that reason I am explicitly stating that I do not accept the general principle as contained in the budget as we know it. I shall therefore oppose the subamendment ; I shall certainly oppose the amendment and I shall vote for the house to go into committee on the budget proposals.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened with much pleasure, as I always do, to the remarks of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen). I feel a good deal as he does, but I have reached a somewhat different conclusion from his. In order to make myself clear I shall state at once how I propose to vote. I propose to vote against the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Fansher) because it contains a principle and a policy which I have always opposed. I am going to vote against the oratorical sentence which is supposed to express the policy of the Conservative party because it leads nowhere and is a mere election phrase. I propose to abstain from voting upon the main motion-

speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext:
-largely for the reasons that have been advanced by the hon. member for Marquette. There are in the budget some features that I approve; there are some that I cannot approve; and the budget as a whole is so involved that I have been unable so far to work out the proportion between good and bad. Therefore I shall do as most of the people in the country will have to do-wait for a month or so of study and discussion before I make up my mind.
The only two features upon which I desire to express my opinion are the proposals styled the countervailing duties, and the increase in

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
the British preference. Both are protectionist measures. One is a measure of Canadian protection and the other is a measure of English or Imperial protection. I have never been a free trader in principle and therefore I do not feel pangs of conscience as some of my hon. friends on this side of the house do in either supporting or opposing this dual protectionist budget.
As regards the countervailing duties I say, perhaps somewhat cynically, that I think they commend themselves to the attention of the house and ought not to be opposed, mainly because they are demanded, not in all parts of the country, but generally by the country; and under our system of government I believe it is the duty of the government to listen to the voice of the people unless that voice demands something absolutely contrary to public interest. Like the hon. member for Marquette I do not believe the imposition of these countervailing duties will relieve the situation of the farmers to the extent that some of them seem to expect. I would rather be inclined to think the suggestion propounded on many occasions by the late member for Laprairie, Mr. Lanctot, namely, the imposition of a seasonal tariff, taking into account differences in climate and therefore differences in production, importation and consumption, would have been a sounder basis for such a policy. Words have been exchanged between both sides of the house as to the principle and the effect of this new policy. Hon. gentlemen opposite have endeavoured to contrast it with the policy once suggested by their former leader, Mr. Meighen. I think they have made a mistake. This policy is precisely Mr. Meighen's policy; it is undoubtedly a brick for brick policy, under a new name. It is like the endeavour in England to conceal the measure of protection that was adopted under the term "safeguarding of industry." It is like the gymnastics into which the various delegates of the Conservative party entered at their Winnipeg convention in order to secure an approval of their fiscal policy without mentioning the word "protection." Of course it is a policy of retaliation. The question is whether it is legitimate or not. The fact that members on that side or this side approved or disapproved of that policy five, ten or twenty-five years ago, has nothing to do with the matter. The question is whether it is the proper policy to adapt now in the interests of the people of Canada. I am not quite sure as to that; but I know that a large and growing number of people in Canada, east and west, in British Columbia, Quebec, Ontario and the maritime provinces, are asking for it. Frankly I would rather have it in
this way than in the form of a general increase in the tariff upon those products. In a sense, it is an open avowal of the futility of our efforts in the past to secure fair treatment from the United States government; but at the same time it leaves the door open to better terms. It has been stated that this is a made-in-Washington tariff. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) especially made a very effective use, so far a3 what I will call skin feeling is concerned, of that expression. Of course that is childish. The brick-for-brick policy of Mr. Meighen was equally a tariff made in Washington.

speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. it meant that Mr. Meighen and his party were prepared to raise our tariff brick for brick as the people of the United States raised theirs. Call it brick for brick, retaliation, countervailing duties, or what you will, the moment that this parliament, which is always master of its acts, decides to change its tariff policy according to changes made by another country, call your policy whatever name you like, baptize it in whatever creed you belong to, the principle is that you change your tariff according to the position taken by another country. And it is not altogether wrong; that is, if you do not make a religion of free trade. I have one religion which I hope is sufficient for the salvation of my soul, provided I make use of it, and I have never tried to make of any economic or political creed a religion. I admit that I am an opportunist in these matters and that I am prepared to change economic policies according to the economic changes that take place in this country and the rest of the world. Therefore, so far as that part of the budget is concerned, I would have no objection in supporting the policy of the government.
Whether it will create a great effect in the United States or not I do not know, and it is no surprise that an ignorant individual like myself should hesitate at pronouncing an opinion upon that point when I find these two contradictory expressions of opinion in the gospel book of the great Tory party. I quote from the first leading editorial on page 12 of the Montreal Gazette of the 12th of May, this short sentence:
United States opinion is that Canada's countervailing duties will do no harm to American trade.
In other words, according to the opinion expressed by the editors of the Montreal Gazette, or imposed upon the editors of the Montreal Gazette by the leader of their party or by the leaders of finance in Montreal,

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
countervailing duties will have no effect upon the exportation of American goods to Canada. But in the same issue of the same paper, on page 13, just the opposite page, I find this message, not a press message, but a message from a special correspondent of the Gazette in Washington:
An analysis of the new Canadian tariff law revised to foster empire trade, which would adversely affect American trade with Canada probably to the amount of $225,000,000, was made public to-night by the Department of Commerce of the United States. The analysis is based on telegraphic despatches from Commercial Attache Lynn W. Meekins, and Assistant Trade Commissioner A. H. Thiemann, at Ottawa.
So here you have in the same issue the opinion that these duties will not affect the trade of the United States, and on the other hand the opinion based on the reports of representatives of the United States in Canada that they will adversely affect American trade to the amount of $225,000,000. Quite a contradiction. The future will demonstrate which of the opinions is right. Nevertheless, I repeat, I think the government did right in this matter, to lend itself to the incessant demand of the fruit producers as well as a large number of farmers, especially those engaged in the dairy industry.
As to the other part of the budget dealing with the British preference, the reason why I shall vote against the subamendment of the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Fan-sher) is the reason why I cannot support this part of the budget. It has been stated by one of our good friends from the west (Mr. McPhee), to whose speech last night I listened with much pleasure, that this is a prolongation of the policy adopted by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding. Well, let us understand which policy, because there were two decisive phases in the adoption and pursuance of that British preference policy. I was in parliament when we passed from one phase to the other and therefore I know a little of what I am talking about.
In 1897, Mr. Fielding brought down in his budget the first preferential tariff ever introduced in this country. Under its provisions, favoured treatment was granted to goods imported from Great Britain and from any other country. British or foreign, offering to Canada special trade advantages. That was, I thought, a good basis for increasing our international trade. Although the British people and the British government granted us no special favours, although they treated our products in the same manner as they treated their imports from all other countries on earth, so
lMr. Bourassa.]
long as Great Britain constituted our best market for our exports I thought that that was a good policy and I supported it.
But in 1900, three years later, in the midst of our first fits of imperial frenzy, at the suggestion of Mr. Russell, then the member for Halifax and now Judge Russell, a dear friend of mine, but a staunch and exalted imperialist, the government changed the basis of their policy. They adopted a three-cornered tariff, so to speak; one tariff applying to Great Britain and other British countries, on grounds of sentiment; another, the intermediate tariff, applying to countries which offered us equal advantages in trade, which was a businesslike principle; and a third tariff applied against all other countries. I could not see why sentiment should be introduced into a policy of that kind, and I voted against it, to the great scandal of my Liberal friends and to the great annoyance of the Tories who did not want to have anything to do with such a heretic as I was. Then and ever since, I stated that as a Canadian I think that the people in the world with whom we have the most interest in dealing are the British people, that they are the finest traders in the world: but also, that the worst manner in which we Canadians or any people on earth can meet the British in matters of trade is to introduce that form of mugwash sentiment which we introduced in 1900, and which has never been reciprocated by the British. Thank heaven, they continue to give us lessons in common sense and in the right spirit of business; and I think that the best way in which we can prove our loyalty to British institutions and British traditions is to trade with the British on the same basis on which they are prepared to trade with us or anybody else. A couple of years afterwards our own people began to open their eyes.

Just wait a second.
Two years later the first fever of love was somewhat abated, the more so because it was not reciprocated. I do not know who it was that said that the most inflamed passion cannot continue to exist unless it is sustained by two parties at least, unless it is reciprocated. At the Imperial conference in 1902, Mr. Fielding, in London, gave warning to

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
Great Britain that unless she treated Canada and her producers in a somewhat different manner from that in which she treated all her other customers, Canada would retrace her steps. But we never retraced our steps. We went on keeping as the basis of our fiscal policy the policy of protection as against most nations, the policy of intermediate tariffs as against nations that offered us trade advantages, and a policy of unreciprocated preferences with regard to Great Britain, whether or not Great Britain gave preferences to the Dominion.
Now, the member for Last Mountain (Mr. Fansher) in introducing his amendment advocated-and the amendment carries out that idea-the granting of still more advantages to British trade, mainly the abrogating of the measure which was introduced last year by this government requiring that so-called British products should contain at least 50 per cent British labour and material. The idea I derived from reading the speech of the hon. gentleman is that if we go still further in that direction, if, for example, we enable the cotton spinners of Lancashire to drown our markets, to ruin our own cotton factories, the good people of the west will have a greater advantage in selling their products in the British market.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman asks us to do away with the requirement that British products should contain at least 50 per cent British labour and material. 1 want to point out the dire illusion under which our western friends labour if they imagine that by doing some further favour to the cotton spinners of Lancashire they will get better treatment from the wheat buyers and millers of England and Scotland.

speechtext: Let me assure the hon. gentleman we have no illusions in that regard.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then what is the reason for the amendment, and why does the government increase the British preference, when there is no apparent sign whatever that the British government is prepared at the present time to grant us any more favourable treatment than it grants to the Germans, to the Italians, to the French, to the Japanese or to the Chinese? In this respect I would ask our
western friends, and my Liberal friends generally to ponder over these paragraphs which were reproduced from the Toronto Star in the Free Press Evening Bulletin of Winnipeg of March 15th last. They appear in a very able review of the wheat situation by a gentleman of the name of Frederick Griffin.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit just one question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If my hon. friend will excuse me: Under the forty minute rule, and having to express views which do not coincide with those of any other group, I am somewhat handicapped.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman leaves a wrong impression.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There will be an opportunity to correct it. I am reading now these paragraphs:
There has been much talk of the British miller-and in Winnipeg someone remarked that there is no one on earth-as hard-headed as the Scottish cooperative miller who figures in this wheat picture. British millers have been blamed for screwing the wheat pool, for being out to smash cooperative selling on the part of the great mass of Canadian farmers.
Perhaps they have been. If they have proven unsentimental, if they have failed to let the alleged imperial tie interfere with the chance to win dividends even to the extent of giving the British consumer at the old price an inferior loaf made from lower grade wheat without the old proportion of Canadian mixing, it must be said that they are merely giving an imitation of Greek meeting Greek. The wheat pool cannot be accused of sentimentality. The Canadian wheat producers have not been worrying much about the imperial effect when trying to extract the last possible cent per bushel from British and European consumers.
This is said without sarcasm. It simply illustrates what the most emotional imperialist knows; that money talks a language that is not so much diplomatic as direct and that no amount of flag-waving can loosen up a pocketbook-at least in peace times.
Great Britain-rather the British millers- simply took advantage of the European situation to turn the tables on Canada. For a number of years they have had to meet Canadian prices, and like it. Now they found the chance to make Canada meet theirs, and like it. All is fair in peace and trade, even between imperial brethren.
Now, this is the exact situation which presented itself at every conference at which those matters were discussed. A giant in mental and political strength compared with the lordly pigmy of to-day-who, thanks to his happy operations in cement-merging in Canada, is endeavouring ito resurrect the old idea of Imperial economic unity-the late Joseph Chamberlain devoted the last years of his life in endeavouring to enthuse the British people over what he called an imperi-

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
ally minded policy. He did not succeed. During the war the Tories of England endeavoured to take advantage of the situation to advance in a more modest manner the idea of imperial economic unity. They failed. And to-day Lord Beaverbrook, with all his genius for cementing and cement, is dragging behind him, but only apparently and only to a certain degree, Mr. Stanley Baldwin. Mr. Baldwin is a shrewd Englishman of the old type, and I believe he will find ways of getting rid of Lord Beaverbrook, just as Mr. Lloyd George found means of getting rid of Lord Northoliffe in due time.
But taking the situation as it presents itself to-day, whether this increase in the British preference-not only without an assurance but without any indication on the part of the British government that they are prepared to do something reciprocally-will gather votes in Canada, I do not know. Apparently it has gathered some votes in West Fulham in favour of the candidate of the new Tory-Imperialist party! But what about the next imperial economic conference, when representatives of this country will go and meet the representatives of Great Britain and the other Dominions or sister nations? I am not quite sure that the Prime Minister of Canada will be any stronger in his dealings with Mr. Ramsay MacDonald by pluming himself on the compliments which he has received from Lord Beaverbrook. As far as I am concerned, disconnected from all parties as I am, there remains enough in me of the old Liberal to oelieve that the Liberal party and the Liberal government in Canada have something else to do than to strengthen the hands of the most Tory-Imperialist wing of the Tory party of England.
That is from the political point of view But from the economic point of view I was surprised to hear a sensible man like the Minister of Finance-one of the members of this house for whom I have the most respect and esteem-sensible Englishman as he is, speaking in that lofty-and childish-fashion of granting gratuitous favours to the poor, down trodden English nation, in no "spirit of petty bargaining." If the British communities to-day stand foremost on the five continents of the world it is not because of their deeds of conquest, it is not because of their political genius or their mental superiority. In all these matters they have had and still have their qualities and their deficiencies. They have committed their crimes and they have done their great deeds. If there is one thing which has made and sustained the greatness of the British nation for the last two centuries it is its bargaining spirit. Lord Rosebery once
[Mr. Bourassa.J
said in effect: "We quite foolishly took to heart for a number of years Napoleon's saying that ' England is a nation of shopkeepers.' Why did we not realize before that our source of greatness is our shopping spirit? The trouble is that so many people have learned our lessons and are becoming shopkeepers that to-day we have to drive the best bargains we can with the nations of the world." This, of course, is not a verbatim quotation.
Likewise, I think the best manner in which Canada can prove herself a true scion of old John Bull, a true chip of the old block, is to meet the British not in a "spirit of petty bargaining" but on a solid ground of fair play and good bargaining. It seems to me that if we wanted to offer some advantages in matters of trade to the British government and to the British people, we should have done as we have done with the Americans: put it on a conditional basis, not on a basis of "petty bargaining" but on a solid basis of fair play and sound bargaining. What reason have we to believe that if we lower all these duties, the British millers, who have for some years struggled with the wheat pool of Canada and have at last obtained the upper hand, are going to cease their purchasing of cheaper wheat in the Argentine and elsewhere, thereby lowering their own profits, just to enable the Lancashire weavers to ship a few more tons of their products to Canada? The British nation as a whole stands first for itself and fair play for others after it has served itself; likewise every branch of British trade and industry stands first for itself. Canada will not meet the English miller by bestowing favours upon the Lancashire cotton maker; Canada will not meet a trader in wheat which purchases in the cheapest market and sells for a profit to the highest bidder, by saying that she has granted favours to the makers of crockery in this or that English town.
It has been said that in order to minimise the emigration of unemployed from Great Britain to our shores we must increase the trade of Great Britain to such an extent that she will be able to keep her people at home. Well, surely nobody has seriously thought of that. The great crisis in Great Britain to-day is because of the fact that she is threatened- I do not say that she is fatally threatened, but I do say that Great Britain is threatened in her position as the trade centre of the world. Great Britain lived, prospered and grew, perhaps abnormally, because of her free trade policy, because of her shipping trade, because of her genius as a trading and travelling nation; she had succeeded in finding out and

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
tapping all the markets of the five continents from which she could draw the raw material necessary to maintain her industries, and to which she sent back her manufactured goods. That is the source of the trouble in India today, and it is the main source of the present Chinese difficulties; it is also one of the sources of the trouble in Russia. England's power is threatened because markets containing over a billion of human beings have cut off her trade; and some people here imagine that because we are going to buy a few more bales of cotton from Great Britain and threaten the existence of a few Canadian manufacturers, we are going to settle the affairs of Great Britain and take the place of all the Indians, Chinese, Russians, Bulgarians, Serbians, Turks, and all those clients of England upon whose trade England has thrived for fifty years, and the bulk of whose trade is now lost to England, or at least greatly handicapped? It is preposterous.
I sympathise with the English; I think the world would be worse if England disappeared, the world would suffer if English power were too greatly weakened. However, it is ridiculous, it is the thought of a parvenu or of a child who has not measured his strength, to imagine that we can settle the affairs of England. Let us rather come back to the thought which has been frequently expressed by the leader of this government and by the Minister of Justice (Mr Lapointe): Let us frame our policy first to suit ourselves, but frame it with an open eye, so that we may deal preferentially with people who are prepared to deal with us. I wish to state that there is no people on earth with whom I would rather deal, or with whom I would rather commune mentally or politically, than the British people:	I refer
of course to the true, broad British people, the British people with the world view. At the same time it is ridiculous to imagine that Britons are going to change their policies in order to suit us and to purchase our wheat. Therefore I think we should make our own conditions to suit ourselves, and approach the situation as we have approached the one affecting the United States. We should approach the English situation in a proper spirit.

rivalry between the two parties as to which would sacrifice Canada for the empire more than the other; and then came the day when a future leader of the Conservative party boasted, and his boast was advertised from the Pacific to the Atlantic, that he was prepared to bankrupt Canada to save the empire.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I may begin what 1
have to say this afternoon by expressing my envy of the two previous speakers. I wish I could approach this subject as they did. I am heartily in accord with the idea advanced by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen); I think it will commend itself to the judgment of this house, and this budget brings the matter right to a head. As the hon. member has said, this budget contains a number of proposals with which members on both sides do not agree. If we could discuss these items among ourselves before being obliged to swallow the budget as a whole I think many of us in this house would be more comfortable this afternoon. For my part, under ordinary circumstances I would hesitate to take up the time of the house at all, but the circumstances surrounding this budget are so peculiar that I feel that I really must make a statement to the house as to the position I intend to take.
I may say in beginning that I think the budget presented this year is without a parallel in Canadian political history, although I understand that there have been two or three occasions in British history when the government of the day simply took the policy which had been advocated by the opposition, made it their own and appealed to the people. This is an exceedingly difficult position; it is a regular paradox to find the government of the day appealing to the people to support them because they are now adopting policies to which they have been opposed for some 
years. It must be confusing to the man on the street, in whose mind the two parties have been associated with particular policies; now he finds that the party with which he associated one set of policies has taken an about face and is appealing for his support on the policies which have been advocated by the opposition. I think the man on the street will be largely influenced by his own judgment, because after all the general level of intelligence in Canada is fairly high. If these policies now being submitted by the government commend themselves to the people, I think the people will see to it that the party which promulgated these policies in the first instance will be the party entrusted with their administration.
Now I want to refer to a statement made by the right hon. Prime Minister on February 24 of this year, which will be found at page 47 of Hansard. He was referring then to the record of his government during the last nine years, and he referred to what he had done for the relief of the maritime provinces. This is what he said:
Reference is made to the maritime provinces. When we came into office we found a condition of unrest in the maritimes. It was the most serious situation with which the country was then faced. We appointed a commission to look into conditions there, and we acted on the report of that commission in very considerable detail. A very little still remains to be done, and I hope that before we are through hon. gentlemen may find that the report has been implemented in all particulars.
The right hon. gentleman overlooked some very salient facts in that connection. This government did come into power in 1921, with a solid contingent of Liberals from the province of Nova Scotia. There was not a Conservative elected from that province, and from 1921 to 1925 the Prime Minister sat in this house with a solid Nova Scotia representation behind him, but not one peep ever came from any member representing that province with regard to the grievances of the maritimes. The Prime Minister was right in saying that there was unrest in the maritimes in 1921, very grievous unrest, which grew until it culminated in the provincial and federal elections of 1925. The provincial Liberal government, which had been in power in Nova Scotia for forty years, was swept into the discard; when it went to the country there were forty Liberals in the house with only three Conservatives, but the figures were reversed after the election.
Then what happened? During the first session of the legislature a resolution was adopted dealing with matters as they then
MAY IS, 1930	2129
The Budget-Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton)
stood in that province, which resolution is to be found at page 51 of the brief prepared by the province. It is as follows:
Whereas Nova Scotia in entering confederation made possible the unification and consolidation of a British Dominion on this continent;
And whereas at that time certain pledges were given that such measures would be undertaken and such policies pursued as would ensure for the future a satisfactory economic position for this province;
And whereas the pledges given ^have been disregarded, as a result of which Nova Scotia has not shared in equal measure the prosperity enjoyed by the Dominion as a whole;
And whereas the government is now engaged in preparing a memorandum setting forth in detail the claims of the province -with the object in view of seeking such adequate redress as wri!l ensure a return of contentment and prosperity to our people;	_
Therefore be it resolved that this house approves of the action now being taken by the government;
And be it further resolved that such memorandum be presented by the government to the federal government, with the assurance that the people of this province believe that adequate remedies exist and must be applied.
That resolution was passed on March 12, 1926. In the speech from the throne delivered in 1926, the government of that day, headed by the present Prime Minister, declared its intention to appoint a commission. That was not our idea of the manner in which to approach this question. The government of Nova Scotia at great cost had prepared an elaborate brief and it was their desire to present that brief to the government. However, there was a difference of opinion; the maritime members insisted tjiat this matter should be presented to the government, and the government and its followers insisted upon the matter being referred to a commission. That commission was appointed some months afterwards, on April 17, 1926, a month or so after this resolution was passed in the provincial house. That commission sat and made its report in September of 1926, and from that day to this the maritime members have been insisting that the recommendations contained in that report should be implemented by this government. Whatever benefits have accrued to the maritime provinces as a result of the Duncan commission are due entirely to the insistent and persistent efforts made by the Conservative members from 1926 onward, and we find one more recommendation being implemented in the present budget. Do not let it be thought that all the recommendations contained in the Duncan report have been implemented; they have not. Some have, and for those I suppose we should be duly grateful, but the adoption of a national fuel policy whereby this country could be made 2419-135
independent of any other country in the matter of fuel has not been decided upon by this government.
I think we were all, and I know I was, rather favourably impressed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in his presentation of the budget on May 1. At that time I thought that the minister had succeeded in putting over a very tricky budget. However, as he delivered his speech and when I saw the demonstrations which followed, I changed my opinion. There were certain provisions in the budget which appealed to members on both sides of the house. There were others which caused considerable surprise, but when I looked at the faces of the hon. gentlemen opposite during the presentation of that budget, if they expressed joyful surprise then I do not know the meaning of the word "consternation." That first favourable impression has been largely discounted. A practice has grown up in recent years amongst certain literary men, known as debunking. Certain gentlemen are pulling down idols which have existed for some time, and destroying traditions which have been handed down for many years. They endeavour to show that the idols have feet of clay, and the traditions have no foundation in fact. The same thing has happened with regard to this budget. A debunking process has been going on ever since it was presented, and it is now found that the whole thing was an illusion.
I was particularly interested in the provisions dealing with the iron and steel industry, but there is not a man living, as far as I can learn, who can give an intelligent interpretation as to the meaning of those provisions. I spent half a day going over the items, but I had to give it up in despair. I got in touch with some of the leading steel executives of this country, but they told me quite frankly that they did not know what they meant and that it would take a year or two to find the real effects. I am in receipt of telegrams which claim that the proposed item 380, which permits fabricated steel to enter this country under the British preferential tariff on payment of 10 per cent duty will put the steel fabricators of Sydney out of business. Other steel executives state that on the whole they are satisfied.
There is one provision in the budget which commends itself to me, that with regard to the payment of a bonus on coal used in iron and steel production. That provision is contained in the last paragraph of the budget speech, which reads:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of forty-nine and one-half cents per ton on bituminous coal mined

The Budget-Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton)
in Canada and converted into coke in Canada and used in the smelting of iron from ore, or in the production of steel.
The very first thing to be noted with regard to that is that it is not in the terms of the Duncan report. Just whether the matter is important or not I do not pretend to say, but there is a strong impression in many places that there is a great difference between the Duncan report recommendations and the reference in the budget speech. The Duncan report states at page 38:
Having regard to the bounty system previously applied, and to this aspect of the application of the drawback, we recommend that a bonus should be given in respect of steel when Canadian coal is used in its manufacture, and that the bonus should be calculated on the basis of the present drawback for every ton of coal used in such manufacture.
As I have said, so far as I am concerned that is the important feature in this budget. What I am going to say now is directed principally to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan). I am sorry he is not in his seat, because what I am going to say is intended to afford him an opportunity, the opportunity of his life, to do something for the labouring men employed in the steel industry of Cape Breton. I want to point out first the ground upon which this bounty is given, the basis for its recommendation. This will be found on page 37 of the Duncan report as follows:
We were asked to recommend that a bounty should be again made available. In this connection we have thought it right to give consideration to a point which was emphasized in the course of the evidence, viz.:-that a drawback of 99 per cent of the duty is given when imported coal is used for metallurgical purposes, and that this is tantamount to giving a bonus of that amount, since it means that the Dominion is yielding up money which otherwise under its general policy in regard to bituminous coal would accrue to it.
The basis of that recommendation is that the Cape Breton steel industry should be put on the same footing as the other Canadian industries. What I want to call the attention of the Minister of Labour to is this, that some of these other Canadian industries are now adopting the eight hour day and if the Cape Breton steel industry is to be put on an even footing with the other Canadian concerns, there should be some provision for the adoption of the eight hour day.
There is another consideration that I desire to offer to the Minister of Labour. During the last three years the steel company at Sydney has been in the hands of a receiver. According to the reports made for that receiver, that concern has been earning more than $2,000,000 a year over its operating expenses. Of course the receiver does not

have to pay any interest on bonds or dividends to stockholders or anything of that sort. That situation is all right for the company, but how about the men employed there, men employed for two or three days a week, men deprived of employment altogether, 600 men thrown out of employment within the last few months, with repeated applications made to the city council of Sydney for relief and to start city work in order to give those people enough to eat. I have in my hand a letter from the president of the Trades and Labour Council who was employed there. He has been working only three days a week and his total pay, January 1 to April 24, has been $144. That man's case is typical; with a family of five he has been working for over three months at less than $40 a month.
The point I want to bring home to the government is this: we have a saying down in our part of the country that there is no necessity for greasing a fat pig. That company is now making money; it has the money in its treasury. Let us see that that money is used for two purposes: first, to increase the wages of the men, and, second, to shorten their hours of labour. There is no excuse in this case of getting behind the constitutional question and saying that the constitution prevents this being done. The government has the money and it can tie it up with whatever strings it wants to when it gives it to the company. This is the opportunity of a lifetime for the Minister of Labour and the government to do something. I represent in this house the workers in that steel industry and I Say to the government without reserve: Let them give me the assurance now that they will devote this money to increasing wages and I will vote for the budget. We have not a minister present who is able to reply. During the whole course of this debate the front benches have been occupied by only one or two ministers, sometimes awake and sometimes asleep. There is no getting away from this challenge. I am not taking anybody by surprise, because to-day I informed the Prime Minister that I would ask him this question across the floor of the house. Let them give me the assurance that they will devote this money or a portion of it to affording these people a living wage and I will vote for the budget; otherwise I will not. This is a serious matter for me. For the first time in twenty-five years my chief and I have had a difference of opinion. He knows and I know how serious that is, but I have to tell him to-day that such will be my course if the government will give me that assurance, and there is no minister present vo give it.

The Budget-Mr. Brown
With regard to the amendment I subscribe to every paragraph of the amendment moved by my leader. I have no confidence in the government, but I am prepared to give them my support on the budget if they will give me that assurance. Either they are going to help the men employed in that concern or they are going to help a concern that does not need it. I am in this position. I am pledged to these men. I have given them my assurance that anything that comes down for their assistance, either steel or coal, will have my support in this house no matter whether it comes from the Grits or the Tories, and that pledge I am going to keep. I know that this party is entitled to whatever credit comes from the implementing of the Duncan report, and I know that when this party comes into power after the next election, as come it will, this portion of the report will be implemented in full, and we will go even further and carry out the recommendations that we all want with regard to a fuel policy. Just now I feel that I want to support this particular clause in the budget, but I connot do so unless I support the whole budget. That is the same point that was raised by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen). I want to support this particular clause, but to do so I have to swallow the whole budget, and I am prepared to do that if the government will give me the assurance that I have asked for. Will they do it?
I rather envy the position taken by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) who has just preceded me. He is going to vote one way on one amendment, one way on another amendment, and then take to the woods on the main motion.

A few days ago the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Bock) who, in spite of the sneers of the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), delivered a speech that had in it more humour and common sense combined than is usually the case with speeches in this house, drew the attention of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) to the fact that certain tactics were being pursued by the Conservative party in the province of Saskatchewan. and he asked the leader of the opposition if he endorsed those tactics. speechtext:
Is it any wonder that it
was circulated in Quebec in view of what is being done in Saskatchewan? The question I want to discuss at the moment, Mr. Speaker, is the question of political patronage. I am asking the leader of the opposition if he has two standards in this matter, one for his friends and one for his opponents. I am moved to discuss this matter because of a letter that appeared in the Ottawa Citizen this week, headed, " Mr. Dickie's Comment:"
To the Editor:-I have always been treated so fairly by your good self that I feel sure you will have corrected a slight inadvertency that crept into an excerpt of a report on my few remarks at Esquimalt Conservative picnic. I said in part: "When our party gets in power, if I am your member, I will at once consult with the various executives of this large constituency; will obtain and assemble their views, and bring my best judgment to bear on them; for most certainly the views of those who have borne the burden and heat of the day when we were out of power should be accorded every consideration. In this way a perfect machine could be built up. and it might be found necessary, as with a ship in distress, to jettison otherwise valuable cargo.
C. H. Dickie.
Victoria, B.C., Aug. 10, 1929.
I did not notice until to-day that it was dated August 10, 1929. I presume the editor of the Citizen had some purpose in reprinting the letter this week. But what I want to say is this, that although that letter is clothed in very euphemistic language, nevertheless it expressed one of the most vicious principles of political patronage. When I was a boy I found in my father's library a book on the Study of Words, by Archbishop Trench. For a good many years I did not bother to look into it. thinking it was one of those dry-as-

dust books that would be of no interest to me. However, when little more than a boy I took occasion one day to read it and I found it an intensely interesting book. There was one chapter on history in words, and I remember there was another chapter on morality in words. I regret that when I went to the library I was not able to find the book, and not having seen it for forty years, perhaps I may be excused if I do not give exact quotations. But that chapter on morality in words has had an influence on my thinking during my whole life. The thought of that great writer on using smooth words to cover up an evil thing was expressed something like this:
How much better is it under all circumstances to use an ugly name for an ugly thing than to use a name that plays fast and loose with the fundamental principles of morality. Better call a thing by its real name than to use a term that glosses it over and makes it appear to be a good thing when it is really evil.

I cannot be led away from my speech to answer questions of that kind. I will say this, however: If you want to consider the question whether Great Britain is granted real preferences, you must consider those preferences as they apply to definite, specific articles. You cannot form a conclusion by dealing in averages, and that is the point I make. I say the fact that this conclusion is invalid is clear from the further fact that averages vary from year to year without changes being made in the tariff. When we are importing goods of various classes in varying quantities, some free and some dutiable; some at a high rate of duty and some at a low rate; some under ad valorem and some under specific duties, it is simply impossible to make any valid statement based upon these averages. The hon. member for Fort William practically admitted the truth of this statement when he pointed out that some people would want to exclude from this calculation the vast amount of free goods coming in from the United States. The hon. member was quite logical in excluding those goods, but he did not go far enough. He should also have taken into account the large amounts of goods which we, in our own interests, bring in from the United States under low tariffs.
Now let me point out that our imports from Great Britain include a large volume of alcoholic liquors, which volume increased from about $4,000,000 in 1918 to over $40,000,000 in 1929. The duty on the $40,000,000 worth of


alcoholic liquor imported from Great Britain during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1929, was almost 819,000,000, or at the rate of approximately 45 per cent. Surely everyone must recognize that because of that particular class of goods, with such a high percentage of duty, the average must be very materially affected. The fact of the matter is that if we exclude alcoholic liquors we will find that the average rate of duty on goods imported from Great Britain is less than the average rate on goods imported from the United States. I am not saying that this is particularly a matter for congratulation or otherwise, but that is the fact as nearly as I can arrive at it.
How would hon. members opposite correct that situation? Will any one of them say that we should correct it by reducing the duty on alcoholic liquors? I am certain the hon. member for Last Mountain will not say so. I know his attitude toward the liquor traffic and I know that his sentiments are very closely allied to my own. While we do not believe in high duties in general I know he does not want to correct what he thinks is an anomaly by lowering the duty on alcoholic liquors. Will any hon. gentleman opposite advocate that this should be done? Surely not.
Then there may be another way to correct it; we might increase the duties on goods coming from the United States. I know that method would appeal to hon. gentlemen immediately opposite, but would it appeal to the hon. member for Last Mountain? I think not. Of course he is aware that large quantities of agricultural implements enter Canada from the United States at very low rates of duty, and these rates are low because we deem it in our best interests that they should be low. Certainly the hon. member for Last Mountain would not wish to correct the situation to which he referred by raising the duty on agricultural implements or on any of those articles which come from the United States at low rates of duty.
I want to place on Hansard some figures bearing upon the subject which I have been discussing, so that hon. members who have endeavoured to follow the trend of my argument may read the figures for themselves and find out whether or not my argument is sound. I believe that the argument I have made to the house is valid in every respect. In 1908 we imported from Great Britain alcoholic liquors to the amount of $4,350,000; in 1915 the importations had grown to 815,770,805, and in 1929 the volume had increased to $40,314,856. The fact that there is a very high rate of duty imposed on this commodity must, of

necessity, have considerable bearing upon the average rate of duty. No valid statement can be made based upon average duties.
I do not propose to detain the house much longer, but I must state that there are some features of the budget which do not appeal to me. As I have said again and again in this house and in the country, protection on agricultural products does not mean anything to the farmer. I have always objected to the imposition of such duties, not because the farmer has not a right to protection-there is no one who has more right-but because he will receive no benefits.

This is shown by the experience of the farmers of the United States. That is the position which I have always taken and I have not changed [DOT]my mind.
The government has to some extent yielded in its decision to give some protection on certain agricultural products. Time will show whether it has acted wisely or unwisely. For my part, I have not changed my opinion as to the expediency of those duties as considered from the farmer's standpoint.
