speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr Speaker, having supported the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), thereby declaring my lack of confidence in the present government, I desire to make a very brief statement with respect to the main motion.
For several years past we on this side of the house have endeavoured to impress upon the government the necessity of extending some protection to the primary steel industry of this country which would at least provide for the industry an equal opportunity in our home markets in competition with the mass production of the highly specialized steel industries of the United States.
We have asked that assistance be given towards the development of the large deposits of low grade iron ore that are known to exist in this country which would enable the primary steel industries to obtain their supplies of raw material in Canada, providing employment for Canadian labour, rather than depending upon a supply from outside Canada, as they do to-day. We have asked for a revision of the steel schedule in the customs tariff; that an adjustment of tariff be made which would afford more adequate protection for some grades and shapes of primary steel now manufactured in this country.

But nothing has been done, and during this time the imports of iron and steel and their products from the United States have enormously increased; the primary steel industries in Canada have been able to operate only part time, and many of our workers have been forced either to go to the United States to seek employment or to be content with working about three days a week. This can best be illustrated by a quotation from the brief submitted before the tariff board by the Algoma Steel Corporation in 1928, which in part reads as follows:
During the seven years (1921 to 1928) our steel-making capacity has been employed only to the extent of 39 per cent of rated capacity, and in only one year did we exceed 50 per cent, viz.: the fiscal year ended June last. The increase in that year was due entirely to the increased demand for standard rails and fastenings.
The salaries and wages paid during this period (1921 to 1928) amounted to $22,501,555.65, or an average of $3,214,507.95 per annum. Assuming full employment for our steel-making capacity, the additional wages paid within our own plant would amount to upwards of $2,000,000 per annum.
This would indicate that had we been given a proper fiscal policy during the past nine years, in my city alone an additional amount of $2,000,000 a year in wages might have been distributed among the workmen there, providing them with more steady employment and comforts for their families which many have not been able to enjoy.
The government now bring down a budget which contains several provisions to which I do not subscribe, but it does provide a certain measure of relief for the steel industry. It contains some things that we have been asking for, but they are several years too late. I am inclined to believe that the provisions contained in this budget have been adopted by the government as a matter of political expediency, and not from conviction, and I have no confidence in this government giving effect to this budget in a way that would be to the best advantage of the people of Canada. However, as the budget provides for certain changes in the customs tariff which will be of advantage to the steel industry in Canada, and on account of a promise which I have made to my constituents that I would support any legislation which would be beneficial to the industry, I, unlike the government in this regard, intend to keep faith with my people, and as a matter of personal honour will support the budget.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. W. JOHNSTONE (Cape Breton North-Victoria):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I represent a Cape Breton constituency. With that island

The Budget-Mr. Simpson
I have been connected for three generations. I was elected as a supporter of the Conservative party. I have just voted for the amendment of that party declaring that, while certain of the proposals submitted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) are acceptable, others represent a betrayal of the confidence of the Canadian people in the previously declared fiscal policy of the government. During my election I promised the men and women amongst whom I live and practise my profession that I would support any government that would give a bounty to coal used as coke in the production of iron and steel as recommended by the Duncan report. That recommendation reads as follows :
It was pointed out to us that, at its inception. the Nova Scotia steel industry enjoyed national aid in the form of a bounty. This system of bounties prevailed for many years. We were asked to recommend that a bounty should be again made available. In this connection we have thought it right to give consideration to a point which was emphasized in the course of the evidence, viz.:-that a drawback of 99 per cent of the duty is given when imported coal is used for metallurgical purposes, and that this is tantamount to giving a bonus of that amount, since it means that the Dominion is yelding up money which otherwise under its general policy in regard to bituminous coal would accrue to it. While there are, no doubt, other angles from which this concession can be regarded, it does in its operation have the effect of a bonus, and it is difficult to see how the same bonus can be denied to native coal.
Having regard to the bounty system previously applied, and to this aspect of the application of the drawback, we recommend that a bonus should be given in respect of steel when Canadian coal is used in its manufacture, and that the bonus should be calculated on the basis of the present drawback for every ton of coal used in such manufacture.
That recommendation was made three years ago last September. I protest against the long delay in giving effect to it. Such delay has caused untold injury to my constituents and their families. But favouring as I do the payment of a bonus as recommended by the Duncan report, as a matter of personal honour I propose to vote for the motion and thereby keep my promise.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately I was not in my seat when the divisions on the subamendment and the amendment were taken, as I did not expect when I left the house at a few minutes to six that any division would be taken until the house resumed at eight o'clock. I merely rise to express my opinion on the main motion and on the amendment and the subamendment. Had I voted I would have voted against
the Conservative amendment and for the subamendment.
As regards the budget, I may say that I was first elected to this house on the principles of low tariff and free trade. I was painfully surprised during my first session to hear the member for, I think it was. Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lavigueur) state that he and his colleagues from Quebec were protectionist. At the time I made perhaps the rather crude remark that at last I knew why Sir Wilfrid Laurier was defeated in 1911; the protectionists in his ranks foreswore their low tariff principles and thus crucified Sir Wilfrid on a cross of protection. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) took exception to that remark of mine and said that it was not reciprocity but another issue which had turned some of the French-Canadians against their chieftain. May I say in regard to Sir Wilfrid Laurier that in 1905 I received a letter from him with respect to free trade, and in my opinion at no time in his long and distinguished career did he show to better advantage than in his defeat in 1911, for on that occasion he went down to defeat because he preferred to stick to his principles rather than continue in power by deserting those principles. In fact the leaven of protection seems to have been permeating the Liberal party ever since 1911. Pope has well said that:
Vice is a monster of so frightful mien,
As, to be hated, needs but to be seen;
Yet seen too oft, familiar with her face,
We first endure, then pity, then embrace.
My hon. friends opposite at one time hated the name of protection, they despised it as something which should not be espoused by their party, but after seeing it for a while they began to endure, then pity, and now we find them embracing it-much to the amusement of my friends to my right.
I am rather sorry, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot support the budget. There are many things in it that I like; but it contains a good many things that I do not like from the standpoint of low tariff or free trade. It looks to me that what Canada needs at the present time is leadership; the leadership of men who have some principles at heart, who believe in those principles, and who carry them out in spite of whatever may happen. Goldsmith, in describing the character of the village preacher, a man whom he admired very much, said that:
He tried each art, reproved each dull delay,
Allured to brighter worlds, and led the way.
I am afraid that at the present time the policies of this government, far from leading the way, have degenerated into an attitude
The Budget-Mr. Ernst

of putting its ear to the ground to see what can best be done to win the next election. I would have been more pleased to see my Liberal friends on the opposite side stick to the principles which they once professed and which Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Sir Richard Cartwright, Alexander Mackenzie and others in this land of ours laid down as Liberal principles-'principles which do not change with the changing times. The square on the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle is equal to the sum of the squares described on the other two sides. No amount of sophistry can ever alter that truth. If the principles upon which the platform of the Liberal party is based are sound, they do not change with the changing times. They do not look for leaders Who will fashion their doctrines to the varying hour.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if hon. gentlemen opposite are expecting from me a declaration to the effect that I am going to support the budget, I may say that some of them, and those in particular who come from the west, should remember the copybook maxim that honesty is the best policy.
The budget has been debated at great length in respect to the main principles which it involves. There are however a few observations that I would like to make. It has been rightly stated that it will not be found palatable to the Canadian people, and I can think of no better illustration of the truth of this statement than to remind hon. members of the difficulty which that master swallower, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) had in swallowing the budget this afternoon. That hon. gentleman is a past master in the art of swallowing everything-even himself. When that hon. gentleman has had such difficulty I wonder how the Canadian people in the main will stomach it at all.
The budget contains many features which lead me to wonder how the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Crerar), who has obtained the portfolio of Minister of Railways in the present cabinet, will justify the vote he will cast in a few minutes in favour of this budget. I cannot understand his position, especially in view of the observations he made in the city of Winnipeg after he became Minister of Railways.

Yes, it is a section of it. The hon. minister in addressing the Liberal club of the city of Winnipeg expressed himself in these terms:
Condemning protective tariffs, Mr. Crerar said protection was a fiscal policy which could work out in no other way than by conferring benefits on certain sections of the community at the expense of the others. The principle of protection was not suited to a new country.
Here is a portion which corresponds very ill with the speech at Woodstock of the Minister of Justice on national unity:
We can't build up eastern cities at the expense of western cities without developing jealousies, suspicions and strife.
In view of some of the provisions in this budget the house has been waiting for manj'' days to hear a declaration from the Minister of Railways as to how he can justify his vote for protection. I cannot help but feel that that hon. gentleman. and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) must have got their heads together and decided that there must be some way out.
At this time I wish to deal with two or three features of the budget which affect my own province. As a very last item in the budget there is tacked on a paragraph dealing with a bounty on coal used in the production of coke for the manufacture of steel. When the Minister of Finance moves that this house go into committee of ways and means, the traditional usage, as I understand it and as I have no doubt the house understands it, is that that committee should provide ways and means for raising supply for His Majesty. Expenditure has no proper place in the budget, it is put in for one purpose only. I was going to say that it is put in for trickery, but it may be that the word "trickery" is unparliamentary; I shall temper my remarks by saying that the bounty resolution is put in for the purpose of diverting the attention of the people of Nova Scotia and causing them to think that their representatives in this house have voted against something for which that province has asked, whereas in reality they have merely voted against a budget which as a whole they cannot possibly swallow.
My hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. MacDonald) made some allusions this

afternoon to the fact that there was no protection for labour. May I make some further reference to the coal and steel industries. The Duncan report recommended that the tariff board be asked to make an investigation into the duty on coal. Has that been done? My hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) pledged himself when he won the by-election in that constituency that he would resign his seat if the Duncan report were not implemented in full at the end of the first session after his election.

Mr. Speaker, I said that I accepted the word of the hon. gentleman. I repeat, however, that the Halifax Herald carried the statement in its pages three years ago, and I would add that I might have been pardoned for quoting it because for three years the statement has not been denied. I have no doubt whatever that the hon. gentleman will go home as the champion of maritime rights, although I have a recollection of seeing the statement made in Montreal that it is only Tory propaganda. I have no doubt that the Minister of National Defence will do likewise. This afternoon my hon. friend from South Cape Breton gave a resume of the fight we have had since 1923 when that grand old veteran the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) was elected to parliament. That is when the fight started. That was the fight which broke the solid sixteen, and never at any time until the Duncan commission made its report did any hon. gentleman opposite make a speech for what were
known as maritime rights. I hold in my hand extracts from the speeches they made during the campaigns of 1925 and 1926. Take, for instance, the running mate of the Minister of National Defence, who was defeated in Halifax in the election of 1926. I refer to Mr. John Murphy, now a member of the harbour commission, who, speaking before the royal commission and giving evidence, gave this as his conception of maritime rights.
Freedom to negotiate our own trade treaties and to buy and sell in whatever markets we can to the best advantage is the only permanent solution of Nova Scotia's problems.

Dealing with maritime rights, Mr. MacMillan touched on local conditions and the government's presentation of the case before the royal commission. I am quoting from the Halifax Chronicle of August 26, 1926, in which appears a report of Mr. MacMillan's remarks at Truro. Dealing with maritime rights he said:
"It is not maritime rights, but maritime wrongs from which we suffer," said the speaker. "First, confederation; second, national policy and third, the rejection of the reciprocity treaty of 1911."
Those were the hon. gentleman's conceptions of maritime rights. Then there was Mr. Ernest Robinson, former member for King's county, who spoke at Kentville on September 14, 1925, and whose remarks are reported in the Morning Chronicle. Speaking of the proposed reduction in freight rates which had been advocated by hon. members on this side of the house, which would enable our products to reach central Canada, he said:
"What have we now in the maritime provinces which we would be likely to send to central Canada? Nothing except coal and fish. It would be all right to put a lower rate on them, but as for butter, eggs, potatoes and apples, they have more than we." Mr. Robinson said he did not believe in taxing one part of Canada in order to pay another.
Then there was Mr. H. J. Logan, at that time the member for Cumberland and now a senator, who spoke in Kentville and whose remarks are reported in the Morning Chronicle of September 14, 1925. Speaking of maritime rights and Mr. Meighen's promise he said:
The Budget-Mr. Ernst

What will he give us? Chapter freight rates? Well, he has intimated that, but has not said so yet. The provinces do not want doles, but simply justice.
Now we have Mr. Robert E. Finn, of recent fame in the by-election in Halifax city, formerly a member of this house, who is reported as follows in the Chronicle of August 9, 1925:
Maritime rights would never have been heard of had not Sir Charles Tupper and his associates in the Conservative party of 1867 been successful in dragging Nova Scotia into confederation. Tupper had sold this province for eighty cents a head and lived to boast of his accomplishment. The work of the Liberal party has been to undo that great wrong.
Those, Mr. Speaker, were the views of these gentlemen during the elections of 1925 and 1926, but now I have no doubt they will climb on the band wagon along with the minister of National Defence and sing " Hail, Hail, the Gang's All Here." But, sir, the people of Nova Scotia will not forget who fought their fight; they will not forget that every major recommendation in that report which relates to the province of Nova Scotia was based on the case prepared by the Rhodes government. Did any hon. gentleman opposite contribute anything to that inquiry? Did any hon. gentleman opposite give evidence before that commission, and if he did what finding was based upon that evidence? Did the Minister of National Defence contribute anything to that inquiry, or the hon. member for Hants-Iiings, or the hon. member for Lunenburg, as he was then?

Ordinarily, for fresh or frozen halibut, mackerel, salmon and swordfish, the duty is two cents per pound. The budget also contains an allusion to a treaty which is to be negotiated with New-

We have everything; we have water powers, minerals, forests, farm lands, fisheries, and we have a fine people. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: This resolution merely deals with definitions in the iron and steel industry which are brought into line with modern practice. The method of measurement is also changed in order to conform with modern practice, the measurements now being expressed in decimals instead of in the old form of sixteenths.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am sorry I cannot agree with the minister. I do not know why he has departed from the old custom of defining measurement by reference to B.W.G.-Birmingham wire gauge. The term B.W.G. has been understood in the trade for a hundred years and more. Everybody on both continents knows exactly what it means. How are the buyers, dealers or users of hoops and sheets to determine the decimal fractions that this resolution provides for in regard to thickness? There are no gauges in general use to-day, so far as I know, that will do it. Going further back than my lifetime, at all events, the measure of thickness of sheets and hoops of iron and steel has been the wire gauge, and such has been recognized universally.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
As I think I stated in
the budget address, the wordings in connection with the iron and steel schedule to which these definitions refer were widely published among those, who like my hon. friend, have knowledge of the business and of its technique. They were asked to criticize and suggest wordings and definitions, and at the public hearings of the tariff board the matter of definition of measurement to which my hon. friend has just referred was fully discussed. I am advised, and in fact the records of the hearings of the board, will, I am sure, bear it out, that all of those engaged in this business desired the decimal method of measurement to be used as being the most up to date and the most generally in use to-day and the most generally in use also in other countries. The request was unanimous that the decimal method should be adopted. I questioned the change myself when the matter was brought to my attention and assured myself on that point. My hon. friend is in disagreement in this respect not only with the majority but practically with all those engaged in the industry itself.

speechtext: (2) Excise duties or excise taxes shall be disregarded in estimating the market value of goods for the purposes of special duty when the goods are entitled to entry under the British preferential tariff, intermediate tariff or any more favourable tariff.

This, I understand, will affect importations from Japan, as Japan enjoys our intermediate tariff. I am given that information as it has been communicated to me.

speechtext:
The situation has been
developing in recent years due to the increased use in many countries of the excise form of taxation, which produces this result in practice: the goods are sold to the home consumers in the country of origin at a higher figure than they are sold for export, for the reason that the excise duty is not chargeable when the goods are exported. That fact automatically brings the goods in question under the dumping section of the Canadian law, and it has the result, so I am advised, of greatly hampering legitimate import business. My hon. friend asks me about the countries. In reply I can tell him offhand that in Japan it applies with reference to silk. In Germany, Czechoslovakia-I am not sure of France-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: France is covered by the treaty.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
exempt only when the goods come from Great Britain, and the amendment seeks to extend that to intermediate countries.
Another point in connection with the matter has recently been drawn to my attention by the chairman of the Ontario liquor commission, Sir Henry Drayton. As the result of his communication I desire to make an addition to the resolution to meet the point raised which, to my mind, is one of some moment. For centuries it has been the custom for Portuguese wines to be imported in wood, by the barrel, into England, and there bottled in bond for export. A year or so ago, through some complaints, it became apparent to the Department of National Revenue that the practice of bottling in bond in England, involving as it did selling by Great Britain to Canada at prices lower than the wines were selling at in England, brought the Portuguese wines bottled in England under the Canadian dumping law. The chairman of the Ontario liquor commission recently asked me to give consideration to the matter, as in his opinion it was quite unfair to impose a dumping duty in connection with a transaction of that kind. I think there is merit in the contention. In his letter to me Sir Henry Drayton states:
The wines are sent to Great Britain for bottling purposes only, so that the more expert work of the British labourer can be taken advantage of. To give a case in point: A case of port, sold to us at 40 shillings, in bond, f.o.b. London, nevertheless has to be valued for the purpose of your customs department at 56 shillings, the 16 shillings representing the customs duties of Great Britain on that port, assuming it to have been taken out of bond and released for domestic consumption in Great Britain.
I may say that similar representations in reference to the matter were made by the High Commissioner for the United Kingdom, Sir William Clark. The point is that we charge duty on customs duties levied by Great Britain, although the customs duties are not levied on the particular wine which is exported from Portugal, bottled in bond in London and bought by the various liquor commissions in Canada. I therefore propose to add this section to resolution No. 2:
2a. Customs duties of the United Kingdom shall be disregarded in estimating the market value of goods for the purposes of special duty when the goods are entitled to entry under the intermediate tariff or any more favourable tariff and are bottled in bond in the United Kingdom and imported direct therefrom.
I think this measure will commend itself to hon. members of the committee as being a very fair one.

There is always the problem of adjusting Canada's general interest with the particular interest of an industry which is entitled to consideration. That is the point one has to weigh in considering all these matters. I have given it the best study of which I am capable and I think the arrangement is a fair one, especially as it is the identical arrangement under which these people operated prior to August 1, 1928. Then they got a species of windfall by reason of an interpretation.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
They got a windfall which
saved them from disaster.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
But which had the effect of reducing the imports from Japan by only $100,000 worth in these lines of goods.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance
is not making a fair deduction from that. He admitted a few moments ago he had not the knowledge to determine that issue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: What issue?

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The issue as to how large
the restriction has been.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I give such figures as
are available.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
But they are not relevant
to the issue. The real issue is that this difference prevented Japan from getting control and command of the Canadian market, and we wish now to maintain the Canadian producer, in view of the peculiar conditions affecting this trade, in as favourable a position as he has been for the last two years.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: The minister quite rightly calls our attention to the fact that Japan is a good customer of ours, but there is one feature he must not overlook, and it is this: Japan is the largest and one might say, the only large producer of raw silk. She produces 85 per cent of the word's supply of raw silk, and we are already, through this manufacture in Canada, a customer of hers in raw silk. Now she wants to supply us with not only the raw silk but the manufactured article also. We cannot buy 'both. If she supplies the manufactured article, she cannot supply the raw silk too. I should like the minister to lay the matter over until we get a little more information. I want to present the figures I have from the manufacturers in reference to this matter.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think the
minister had better accede to that request. I understand our object in discussing these details in committee is for the purpose of getting all the information we can as to the effect of the changes. The minister himself says he does not know exactly what articles will come under the proposed clause. The department ought to provide a list of the articles that will be affected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: From all countries?

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
From all countries, and the different kinds of articles, so that we may see how many there are. The minister makes a change in the tariff in general terms and he does not know exactly how it will work out. If we had before us a list of importations from all the different countries which would be affected by the proposed change in the method of computing the duties, we could see for ourselves what difference this was going to make, what articles
would be affected, and to what extent. The object of this discussion in committee is to enable us to become better informed than we are now as to what the effect of this change will be on the revenue and an the manufacture of similar articles in this country. I should think the minister himself would want to have the artificial silk manufactured in Canada, provided that the people who make it did not exploit the public and obtain too large a profit out of it. Surely we can make artificial silk in this Dominion as well as any other country in the world. Then why should we facilitate the importation of it as the minister says we are doing under this particular clause? The minister has not told us yet at whose suggestion this change was made. What interests have asked for it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Very many importers
from all countries in connection with importations which in their aggregate value are small as compared with the whole trade of Canada. But as to finding out just what commodities from all countries are affected, my hon. friend can understand that was a natural question for me to ask a moment or two ago. And the answer is, when one thinks it out: This would involve a search of the customs and excise laws of all countries, some of which laws change very rapidly in these days, and then an endeavour to trace the extent to which the particular change in the particular country has been applicable to imports into this country since August 1, 1928. Perhaps it will help my hon. friend if I give the details making up the figure which I gave a moment ago. The impression appears to be abroad that we are importing more manufactured silk. I know that my hon. friend from Lincoln has in mind specific cases along that line. As to the aggregate difference between the two years during one of which the old regulation was in force, we are really seeking to restore what was the practice from 1919 to 1928.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That will naturally have
the effect of restoring the business to where it was before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
bear with me, between the two years in question we have an exact comparison as to what happens when the regulation in force prior to the 1st of May is operative and when it is not. Take raw silk. We imported more raw silk in 1929 than in 1928; $1,200,000 in 1928, and $2,000,000 in 1929. Silk woven in the gum, which I am advised by the people to whom my hon. friend refers is the important item, came in to the amount of $3,088,000 in 1928, and $2,910,000 in 1929, or a
2156	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
difference of only $100,000 or thereabouts. Of silk fabrics we imported in 1928, $3,500,000, and in 1929, $2,700,000; silk clothing, $158,000 in 1928, and $261,000 in 1929.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The fabrics show a very
great reduction in 1929 below 1928.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Then take silk manufactures. There were only small importations; $87,000 in 1928, and $76,000 in 1929; other silk goods, $160,000 in 1928, $155,000 in 1929
Those are all the silk imports from Japan, making up the aggregate totals that I gave before of $8,250,000 in 1928, and $8,145,000 in 1929. I give that just by way of information, hoping that it is the information my hon. friend wants.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I had that information
myself out of the returns. The information I have gives the monthly imports in the lines in which these people are interested, and shows positively that during the six months after the regulations were put into force there was a decided decrease in the importation of these flat goods in which we are interested. But I will admit that in respect to the whole year the amount given by the minister is right.
Mr, DUNNING:	That is the important
thing. My hon. friend knows that it is seasonal importation.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Seasonal importation? I
will show the minister what happened in one month of one year and in the following month of another year, and so on for the six months, and I will prove my contention to him. All I ask is an opportunity to do so.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The language used in this
resolution is very general. When you speak of exicse taxes on goods imported into this country, that might have a very wide meaning. What about Scotch whiskey, for instance, or Guinness' stout? Is an excise tax not collected on these articles before they are exported from Scotland or England, and would they not be affected by this resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friend forgets
that under the present law, which we are now amending, goods from the United Kingdom such as Scotch whiskey are already exempt from excise in the computation of their value under paragraph (b) of section 6 of the customs tariff. Goods of a class subject to excise duty in Canada are now exempt.
My hon. friend spoke of a devious way of doing this. If I had desired to do it in a devious way, all I had to do was to put an excise tax, however small, on silk in Canada, and then under the provisions of that subsection the same object would have been ac-

complished, but I preferred to deal with the matter -as a matter of principle. Also the complaint is made to me by importers that as far as possible the Canadian customs tariff should tell people what duty they have to pay on the goods they import. I think there is a great deal of merit in that contention, in so far as we can accomplish that objective.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: You are not doing that in connection with the countervailing duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes, we are.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: From the explanation made by the minister, it seems that this is a change made for the jobbers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: For those who are bringing in job lots.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, the largest importers in the country made -representations, people like Eaton's and Simpson's.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes, but what are Eaton's but the -largest jobbers in the country? They are not manufacturers. They have no interest in production in this country. They h-ave no interest in the large employment of labour in this country. They are people who simply fatten upon the cheap wages of foreign countries, and then supply the Canadian consumer with the cheap goods from foreign countries with which the producers of Canada, who pay a legitimate wage and have reasonable hours of labour, cannot possibly compete.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Apparently the hon. gentleman never buys anything from Eaton's. I do not find them selling that kind of cheap goods.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Ah, don't you? Of course they do not sell them cheap; they make a profit. If the consumer profited by the jobber's control, I would have something to say in favour of this change; but the jobber makes a profit and the consumer never re-cives the advantage of a single one per cent, and Canadian industry suffers and is finally destroyed. This seems to me to be the most haphazard suggestion that could possibly be made. The minister admits that he does not know the extent of its application; he does not know to what countries it applies: he does not know to what imported commodities it will apply. Certainly in a matter of this kind which affects the vital interest of one great industry in Canada we should have more complete information, and the minister

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
might well hold this over for a day, at least until my hon. friend (Mr. Chaplin) has had an opportunity to obtain his statistics. If the minister insists on going on; we can easily talk it out for ten minutes; but we do not wish to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do not intend in any way to compel my hon. friends to talk out the item. I want to be as courteous as I can if they want the item deferred. I am sure my hon. friends want to cooperate with me in this rather heavy task.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: We do, but this is a vital industry in the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It would, however, be
rather confusing, where there are such a large number of items, if we adopted the practice of leaving some of them over. I am anxious that there should not be errors in the final conclusion of our work, but in this matter I shall try to meet my hon. friends.
My hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George has said that the minister does not know what will be the effect, and so forth. May I repeat that Canada established definitely, by regulation of the Customs department in 1919, the policy which I am now seeking to have embodied in the law. It was discovered only in August of 1908 that what I now contend should be law was not the law, after ten years' experience. So far as I know, no one asked for a ruling bringing into effect the condition which should have obtained since August of 1928 until to-day. The test of experience of the degree of complaint during that ten year period is surely evident that on the matter of principles we are on sound ground. It is, as my hon. friend states, virtually impossible to search the excise laws of all countries just to find out what commodities, if they did come into Canada, would be affected by this provision. I can only say that by this provision Canada goes back to exactly the position she occupied prior to August 1. 1928, and during all those years no one, as far as I know, in this house or outside of it ever made any complaint as to the manner in which the provision was administered. There is just a legal technicality upon which the change was made. I will let the resolution stand, Mr. Chairman, and pass along to the next one.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Might I suggest
that the minister endeavour to get as much information as he can as to what articles will be affected by this change?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Between now and tomorrow afternoon I will get as much information as is available. I cannot undertake that it will be complete, because to search through the excise laws of all countries would involve a very great deal of work.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Might I suggest
that the resolution stand until Monday if my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) is to be here when it is further discussed. '

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: When there are so many items to be dealt with it is hardly fair to ask that they stand over while hon. members are absent. However, we will let the item stand now, and I will try to meet my hon. friend's convenience to the fullest extent.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I would suggest to the
minister that to-morrow he come prepared to give the house this information:	What class
of importers made the request for this change? Are they confined entirely to the silk industry, or do they include others? What countries will be affected and the amount of trade involved?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: I may say, Mr. Chairman, that the numbers have been carefully checked, and there are two typographical errors. After the figure 109 in the fourth line of figures insert the figure 139; this was dropped by the printer. Also, over the page, after the figure 502b insert the figure 502c; this again was dropped by the printer.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will all the items referred to in these different tariff numbers be covered in the new schedule?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
In other words, does the
new schedule omit some of the tariff items which originally stood under the headings of these particular tariff items?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: No, everything is covered. Certain items are before the committee of ways and means because of the fact that it was necessary to change the numbers, and the simplest way to get it before the committee was to wipe out the old numbers and start with the new schedules; but I can assure my hon. friend that everything covered in the items to be wiped out is being dealt with in the new proposals.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: If, for instance, any particular article were imported under No. 10, how are we going to find out under what number in the new schedule that article is being imported?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: If my hon. friend will look at the manner in which the tariff changes this year are set out in the booklet,-which I think he holds in his hand-he will find two sets of three columns each, the first three columns being the present tariff proposals, and the second three the old tariff items. The old tariff item numbers are there given and the rates. So he will be able to get any information as to any item by referring to the list. This year I arranged to have the list incorporated in Hansard so that there would be easily available to every hon. member a comparison between the old and the new.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Do I understand that every item stricken out will be found in some place?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Every commodity in the previous items is dealt with, yes.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have before me a letter from a music publishing firm in Toronto-a copy of which was sent to the minister-asking that item 475 be extended to the music printing industry, because at the present time [The Chairman.]
only a very small part of the music used in Canada is printed here. This would encourage the printing of music in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: I may say that I have the letter before me, but it would help a lot if the discussion could be on the item itself.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Shall the resolution
carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
this resolution covers pages and pages of items. If we say the resolution is carried, that will include all the schedule. I presume we shall take the resolution item by item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: When I said "carried" I referred merely to that part of the resolution which rescinds the various tariff items there enumerated.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: All these schedules are part of resolution 3.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: So all we have done is to carry the first part, the deleting part of the resolution.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Quite so. Now we start with the schedules.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes. I think the usual practice i3 to carry each article separately and finally the complete resolution. I move that the committee rise and report progress.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Before the committee rises, may I ask the minister if there is any objection to laying on the table representations made by Canadian silk factories in reference to this change proposed in the second resolution? Are those representations confidential, or may they not be published?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Some are, but I know of no reason why such representations as we have should not be tabled; although I may tell my hon. friend there are reams and reams of correspondence about these various tariff items.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am dealing simply with resolution No. 2 as to excise duties or excise taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CUSTOMS TAKIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If my hon. friend desires the correspondence I will try to see that he gets it, so far as it is not confidential.
Progress reported.
